## CMS-01 CMS version disclosure reviewed

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Generator version strings help fingerprint a CMS. They may be stale or customized, and do not establish an exploitable vulnerability. Asset query parameters can be cache keys rather than installed core versions.

### Build rule

Keep the CMS patched first. If version disclosure is unnecessary, remove the generator tag using the CMS's supported hook or template configuration. Avoid stripping cache-version parameters without checking caching behavior.

### Proof test

1. Read only pages already returned by the shared crawl. Inspect at most 400,000 characters, 4,000 tokens and 4,096 characters per tag per page; parse generator attributes regardless of order or quoting.
2. Fail (low): a generator discloses a numeric major.minor version string. This proves disclosure only. WordPress core asset ver= values are hints and require manual review.
3. Pass: CMS markers found, no version in the inspected generator tags, and parsing limits were not reached. Manual: no CMS markers, ambiguous values, asset version hints, or parsing limits. Script/comment examples do not establish a generator version.

### Sources

- [WordPress developer docs: wp_generator()](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_generator/)
- [OWASP WSTG: Fingerprint Web Application Framework](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/stable/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/01-Information_Gathering/08-Fingerprint_Web_Application_Framework)

## CMS-02 CMS core on a supported release line

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1104 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Vendor-ended CMS release lines no longer receive upstream security fixes. Public generator metadata is only a claim about the installation; confirm the installed version before remediation. A supported minor line does not establish that security patches are installed.

### Build rule

Install the latest security patches on a currently supported minor release. The 2026-11-07 snapshot records WordPress 7.1; Drupal 11.3, 11.4 and the older 10.6 line; Joomla 6.2 and the older 5.4 line. Recheck vendor schedules: Drupal 10 ends on 2026-12-09 and Joomla 5 security support ends on 2027-10-12. Older WordPress lines may receive courtesy updates, but are not the actively maintained line.

### Proof test

1. Use an unambiguous numeric generator version from the existing crawl; never infer a version from Drupal.settings or asset query parameters.
2. Compare only explicit known minor ranges against the static vendor snapshot dated 2026-11-07. Fail: a generator reports a known vendor-ended line (Drupal 7–9, Drupal 10.0–10.5 or 11.0–11.2, Joomla 3/4 or superseded Joomla 5/6 minors). Warn: an older known line (WordPress 3–6 or 7.0, Drupal 10.6, Joomla 5.4). Warn also: a supported line below its latest known patch (WordPress 7.1.0 when 7.1.4 is known; a bare `7.1` counts as 7.1.0). Pass: the reported version is the latest known patch of a line supported at the snapshot date. Manual: once the snapshot is more than 90 days old ("support data stale"), except that a vendor-ended line still fails.
3. Manual: missing, conflicting, prerelease, major-only or unknown versions, unknown patch numbers, newer lines, or parsing limits. Patch bounds are recorded for WordPress 6.9/7.0/7.1, Drupal 10.6/11.3/11.4 and Joomla 5.4/6.2; other historical nonzero patch numbers require review. Skip: no self-hosted CMS marker. Confirm the installed version and current vendor guidance in the admin dashboard.

### Sources

- [WordPress releases](https://wordpress.org/download/releases/)
- [Drupal core release schedule](https://www.drupal.org/about/core/policies/core-release-cycles/schedule)
- [Drupal core releases](https://www.drupal.org/project/drupal/releases)
- [Joomla roadmap](https://developer.joomla.org/roadmap.html)
- [Joomla support policy: latest minor within each major](https://developer.joomla.org/component/content/article/586-joomla-development-strategy.html)
- [Joomla CMS versions and support dates](https://docs.joomla.org/Joomla%21_CMS_versions/en)

## CMS-03 WordPress REST and XML-RPC exposure needs review

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200, CWE-307 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Public API fields and XML-RPC methods need an intentional access policy and abuse controls. Public author metadata may be intentional. Page links and headers do not establish endpoint access, configuration, or vulnerability.

### Build rule

Review intended public author fields and installed integrations before restricting REST or XML-RPC. Require authentication for private data and protect authentication methods against abuse. If XML-RPC is unused, block it at the server or CDN. The xmlrpc_enabled filter controls authenticated methods, not every XML-RPC method such as pingbacks.

### Proof test

1. Read the shared crawl only; never request /wp-json/ or /xmlrpc.php.
2. Record REST discovery, pingback and EditURI links and the presence of an X-Pingback header without assuming its destination.
3. Always manual when WordPress is detected, even with no markers. Review intended API data, enabled methods, authentication and abuse controls on a site you own. Skip when WordPress is not detected.

### Sources

- [WordPress REST API handbook: Users endpoint](https://developer.wordpress.org/rest-api/reference/users/)
- [WordPress developer docs: xmlrpc_enabled filter](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/hooks/xmlrpc_enabled/)

## CMS-04 Public CMS login links reviewed

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-307 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Public login links identify an authentication surface. Their presence is not a vulnerability; default CMS login paths can be found without links. Authentication and abuse controls determine the actual risk.

### Build rule

Protect CMS authentication with MFA and rate limiting. Apply access restrictions appropriate to the site. Remove unnecessary administrative links if useful, while preserving legitimate user login flows.

### Proof test

1. Inspect same-origin links and form actions in the existing crawl for wp-login.php, wp-admin, administrator and user/login paths. Ignore external and malformed URLs; evidence omits queries and fragments.
2. Manual: a possible login link is present, the CMS is unidentified, or parsing limits were reached. A marker never proves weak authentication. Pass: CMS markers found and no such link in the inspected pages; this says nothing about login protection.

### Sources

- [WordPress hardening](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/security/hardening/)
- [OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html)
